paragraphs.source_en: Lady Chaa knew that Tadateru had made many enemies. The shogun’s close retainers, led by Doi Toshikatsu, still believed Tadateru harbored rebellious ambitions, refused to submit to the honest and upright shogun’s discipline, and sought to occupy Osaka Castle and command the realm. Ieyasu surely knew all this and was therefore patiently awaiting a chance to speak of Tadateru. Yet before Ieyasu had said anything, his condition had already become critical.

paragraphs.source_en: From the twelfth until the morning of the thirteenth, Lady Chaa wrestled repeatedly with the matter before finally deciding to send a messenger to Fukaya. If she did not tell her son the truth, she would fail in her duty both as a mother and as a wife.

paragraphs.source_en: Since his confinement at Fukaya, Tadateru’s disposition had changed greatly. His former imperiousness had vanished, and he no longer wished to dictate to his elder brother. His mind had broadened, his thoughts deepened by the day, and he had learned to observe and reflect calmly upon the human heart. But for that very reason, Lady Chaa felt all the more pain for him.

paragraphs.source_en: Perhaps driven by a dark premonition, Tadateru had been unable to wait for word from his mother. On the road from Kanbara to Sunpu, there was nowhere he could rest in secret except Seikenji at Okitsu. How could he have slipped away on his own?
